utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll first give the ruling of the Chamber on the complaint by the accused. The Chamber received a complaint from Mr. Milosevic that the Registrar had refused to allow him to meet with a prospective witness, Mr. Seselj. We ordered the Registrar to file a report, which he did, on the 7th July, and we have also had submissions from the assigned counsel and the Prosecution. The Chamber notes that the accused has already spent some 20 hours proofing Mr. Seselj. In paragraph 13 of the Registrar's report, he says that he would consider one further request from the accused to proof Mr. Seselj once his name appears on the witness schedule. Mr. Seselj's name now appears on the witness list. Accordingly, Mr. Milosevic should submit a request to the Registrar. The Trial Chamber notes that it does not consider any of the procedures set out in paragraph 17 of the Registrar's report to be contrary to its order of the 17 September 2003. However, it does consider unnecessary the disconnection of the phone and fax facilities of the accused for 24 hours after the proofing session. That's the ruling. I turn next to the motion by Serbia and Montenegro, and we will go into a private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I return to the sequence of events, Mr. Delic, can you help me with one matter of methodology? The materials produced by the group of senior officers round the table included the statements of various people including your subordinate officers. How were those statements prepared by the individual officers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for myself personally, I wrote my statements several days. As for those persons who are in Belgrade, and there is three or four of them, they wrote their statements -- actually, we were in my office so they could have a look at the maps and the orders. They wrote their statements at their own places of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did they do, so far as you understood it, research and further reading at their own places of work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every one of them wrote their own statements to the best of their recollection and using this documentation that was from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they brought a statement and -- let me just take one second. Do you understand the importance of this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're seeking to lay before the Chamber statements of people whom the Chamber may never see that go to show that the allegations of crime against this accused may not be established. So it's important for us to know precisely how the statements were prepared.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're trying to say when you say statements that they had never seen. Who does this pertain to actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something in translation. I'm trying to explain to you the importance. The statements that your colleagues prepared, you'll remember them, they come from Celine and Suva Reka and so on, are statements that it's being asked the Judges should look at and read and take into account in deciding whether these crimes have been committed, although they, the learned Judges, will never see the makers, or may never see the makers of the statements, the people who wrote the statements. So in those circumstances, it's very important to know how the statements were actually prepared. Now, from what you've told us, but don't -- you know, don't say something unless you're quite sure it's correct. From what you've told us, the individual officers, your subordinates and associates, wrote their own statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly correct. If Mr. Milosevic calls all these officers, they will all appear here at least for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any question of the statements being prepared in a collective way, round the table, being written in a committee, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Everyone wrote his own statement. All these officers have had their obligation to guard state secrets waived by the government and they are free to appear before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And having made their individual statements, was there any question of the statements being edited, corrected, added to by a supervising or central body, or did the statements that we've got -- or are the statements that we've got exactly as the officers wrote them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those officers wrote their statements and signed their statements. So by their signatures they confirmed that what is stated in the statements are their own words. I myself wrote my own statement, and I'm responsible for the statement I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously this morning I'm going to have to abandon a large number of papers that -- pages that I might have turned to if we are to complete this witness's testimony before the summer break, allowing reasonable time for re-examination, and I'm going to make points very shortly, and I hope the witness will understand that short answers will be of value to the Chamber. We were at volume 2 of the exhibits, tab 104. I have one question in respect of tab 111, which is a recurring issue, but I need only ask it the once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please, at tab 111. This is an apparently contemporaneous document coming from your motorised brigade, and there are two things about it. First, it is only an extract, you see? Now, why have we only been provided with an extract? Why haven't we been provided with the whole document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document from my brigade. This is a daily report of the security organs for the 10th of August, 1998. This is an extract that pertains to my zone. It has to do with my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the accuracy is verified by --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you really to listen carefully to the questions so that we can save time. May we take it, then, that the other parts of the report which we have not been provided with would relate to other parts of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since daily reports of security organs are made according to certain points, there must be several points there, and they also pertain to other zones in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing on this document, and it recurs throughout the similar documents is, if we look down towards the bottom of the page on the original, and we can see it reflected in the translation, there are passages that have been redacted. We can see two such passages on either side of the word "podaci" I think it is. Is this names of individuals that have been redacted in the way that you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are names of informers of the security service, and that was blanked out in order to protect them. Mr. Nice, you received this document in 2003, you as the Office of the Prosecutor. You got this in a completely different case, all these documents that are here, as far back as in 2003. Your investigator in Belgrade assessed these documents as relevant when they were shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your honour, that's not something that we're in any position to accept at all, but I'm not going to debate it with this witness. Right. If we just look perhaps very briefly at 136. And, Your Honours, just so that I can flesh out my last observation, yes, material was provided that related to wrongdoing or structures of the KLA, but the other material was not provided, that is material that relates to the allegations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 136 is a 9th of September 1998 document signed by Pavkovic, and it says in the middle of the first page in the English: "The foreign media and some journalists are putting forward a theory about the humanitarian catastrophe of the Siptar population, attempting to get world public opinion to put pressure on the Federal Republic and its leadership to halt MUP operations against terrorist strongholds ..." Is it really your view and was it perhaps, as it were, the collective view of the army that somehow the Albanians had completely deceived -- Kosovo Albanians completely deceived the world's press into believing that things were other than they were?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you read a sentence and you stop midway. You're supposed to end the sentence. So you stopped in half sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You and a lot of the other witnesses take standard form responses to my questions. I don't know if you've been asked to do that, but would you please be good enough to listen to the question and answer it. If you want to give it a broader context, do, but please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no humanitarian catastrophe. The foreign media reported very partially about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, my question, to which you did not respond, is was it your view and perhaps the view of the army that the Kosovo Albanians had managed to deceive the world's press?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with Kosovo Albanians. Everything that was done in my country was done according to a scenario that was devised outside of Kosovo and Metohija and outside Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who were the planners and who were the other conspirators or whatever it was that led to misunderstanding and deception of the world's press? You better tell us. We need to know.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known who the persons who had power in the world were at the time. Everything that happened in my country is derived from America and partly from Germany. Do you want me to give you evidence to support that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, but I'm interested to know what your view is. It can be taken further, if necessary, in the examination.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you don't want evidence but you want my view. My view is totally irrelevant if there is evidence supporting what I'm saying. I want to answer your question by providing evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Just identify what this evidence is, then, that shows America and Germany and everybody else, I suppose, involved was misleading the world about what was happening. For the record, you're reading from some notes, and you produced a book from your briefcase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us know what you're reading from, General, if you're going to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from a book written by Mr. Wesley Clark, who was also a witness in this courtroom. It's called "Modern Warfare." I would like all of this to be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd prefer not to take our time with this. He's identified his source, it's a public source. He can identify the pages if he wishes, but I would have thought it would be appropriate, now knowing his state of mind, to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't find all of this very profitable at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It arises from the questions. If you're going to ask questions like this, you're going to get answers. I remind the Prosecution that one of their witnesses said the same thing. Witness Stijovic gave evidence on the 5th of September 2002, and in answer to Judge Kwon's questioning of him he said there were the staged processes by which the Kosovo Albanians had periodically brought their issues to the world attention. But if you're going to ask questions like this, you're going to get answers like that, and you have to be careful. You just can't cut the witness off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move to -- I think we've looked at tab 154, so if we can move now to volume 3, which I can deal with very swiftly. I can deal with -- yes. Indeed, I'm wondering if I need -- I think -- no. I think possibly -- oh, yes. Perhaps just one -- one reference to tab 216. Now, this is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a video, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. And I'm looking at my notes in respect of that and that's why I'm opening it there, and I'm reminding the Court about it in sequence, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the video, is it not, Mr. Delic, where people were seen to have been killed and then there were the survivors who were in the snow. Is that the correct video that I'm dealing with?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we see that video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember the video, the video in the snow? And your evidence about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he doesn't remember it, then he's entitled to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I remember, but is that the video dated the 14th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the video where there were three events in the morning, 2.30, 4.00, and 5.30, and this was the video where the KVM attended, and your evidence, I think, was to the effect that they had a chance of talking to the surviving KLA prisoners. And my simple question to you is this, and it's not one of great weight but I'll just deal with it for detail in light of the evidence we've got: I didn't see, I think, on the film that we saw personal contact between the KVM and the prisoners. Do you remember that there was in fact shown no such contact?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember everything that was shown on that video. There is no contact or no conversation on that video, but the verifiers can be seen, and the prisoners next to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidence that we've been given, I think, is to this effect: That the prisoners were taken away. They were young prisoners. Indeed they were described, I think, in the Prosecution evidence, as showing signs of being unwilling in what they were doing, and they were subsequently seen in detention but sometime after the 15th of January of 1999 by the witness Ciaglinski. Does that accord with your recollection, that the KVM may have been allowed to see these prisoners but at a later stage and talked to them then?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski was not there on the spot. There were two teams from RC1 Prizren. They talked to the prisoners. Those prisoners were not as you describe, young boys or young men, whatever you called them. Mr. Ciaglinski talked to them, but that was in the military prison in Nis, perhaps 15 or 20 days after the event when they were transferred to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very much?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- martial courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... recollection of events, you are indeed confirming the evidence that General Drewienkiewicz gave to the effect that they were seen in prison. Thank you. Can we look, before we turn from 1998, at clip 15 of the video Serb Version of the Split, and this is another --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to protest against this alchemy that Mr. Nice is using. He is noting that the witness confirmed the testimony of Mr. Ciaglinski about what he had seen in prison, but he's not allowing him to say anything else. In fact, the witness refuted the evidence given by Ciaglinski, who lied, just as Ashdown did, and we saw exactly what happened with the prisoners in the footage. I cannot understand that the truth is being allowed to be twisted like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see why you won't let me get a word in edgeways, I'm not confirming what Mr. Drewienkiewicz said. I'm not confirming what he said, but I can confirm that Mr. Ciaglinski was in Nis. But I'm not confirming his testimony related to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. I've heard Your Honour's point but I'm not going to press because we don't have time. Could we look just then, please, at clip 15 of The Serb Version of the Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, that's Pavkovic talking about Ambassador Walker, and he says that the biggest deceit was that they were able to bring in new forces, that is new forces in breach of the October agreements. Does that accord with your recollection, that it was possible, as Pavkovic says, at the end of 1998, to bring in these additional forces in front of Walker's nose, as he says?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my zone there were no additional forces apart from my own forces. There were only my own forces and the forces of the MUP based in that territory. As for Mr. Walker, we knew what his role was, and we had proclaimed that gentleman persona non grata. However, under the pressure of the international community, he stayed there, not to help our country but to prepare an aggression against it, and he accomplished his mission successfully. He had a lot of experience from Latin America, from Salvador where he prepared and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Understand, Mr. Delic, this is not responsive to my question which was about bringing in additional forces, and we have your answer on that. But is this passage of the film Serb Version of the Split a passage like the others that you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I saw this excerpt before because General Pavkovic appeared on many documentary programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have no reason to doubt, do you, what your commander said was the reality at the end of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This did not happen in 1998. In February, we already knew that an aggression against our country was a certainty. This was going on in the first days of March and in the middle of March when we knew that an aggression will certainly be mounted against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It's not just a question of not doubting what Pavkovic says, you actually know what he says is true, but I put the wrong date. It's a little later on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my zone is concerned, what I said is true. No additional forces came in. What General Pavkovic said relates to the period of March. We are military professionals. Of course we would not allow ourselves to be surprised. Regardless of the fact that the United Nations did not approve an intervention in our country, it was being prepared in our immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there unless there's a part of my question you haven't answered.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered all your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As well as preparing, if you say it was February or March, early March, for the consequences of --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: End February until the middle of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What preparations had you made for refugees and other --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in Kosovo there were no displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At what time were there no displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time you are referring to. Before the aggression there was only, in the area of Drenica, a number of internally displaced people whom the terrorists would not let return to their villages. There were no other displaced persons. Everybody was in their homes in their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that point and since you raise it, just have a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was part of Exhibit 234. And if Mr. Prendergast would be good enough to go simply to the table on the fourth page and display that on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you're being invited to look at, Mr. Delic, is a document published by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and the table, I'll read out the title so that you can hear it: "Kosovo displacement statistics from March 1998 to the 24th of March, 1999." And what it deals with is displaced persons in Serbia, then in Kosovo, then in Montenegro, and then it deals with refugees. Staying with the second column, it suggests figures of 24.000 in March 1998, 17.000 in April, for Kosovo, and then running down through 1998 we come down to 200.000 displaced in October, 175.000 in November and December, and then 190 in January, 210 in February, and then rising in March. Do you -- you were on the ground. Do you accept in general terms that those statistics prepared by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees are correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now be talking about my own area. This is not shown area by area. It's shown for the entire Kosovo and Metohija. In my area, there were no displaced persons. Everybody returned to their villages. I know there was a number of displaced persons, especially in the area of Drenica, but if you take the entire population of Drenica and gather them in one place, that would still be four times less than the figure indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the figure --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These figures are quite exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. You say the figures are exaggerated. We had a Prosecution -- a Defence witness, Primakov -- I haven't got the exhibit to hand, we'll find it -- the Russian senior politician who prepared -- who was party to reports that were tendered at the United Nations, showing very large numbers of Albanians displaced in the second half of 1998. I'll get the figures if I can. Do you not accept that there were very large numbers of people displaced internally in the second half of 1998 in Kosovo even if not in your area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say a large number, I would like you to specify. What do you mean by a large number? And second, I would like to hear whether the state authorities of the Republic of Serbia participated in the collection of this data. I'm saying again these figures are overblown by about four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That's your answer. We're going to move on. If we just look at Exhibit 252 - it will only take a second. Tab 252, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that. Mr. Delic, if these figures were correct, and obviously if they've been produced by both the Prosecution and the Defence, then -- if that's the case, then considerable weight has to be given to them at least in our deliberations before deciding what to make of them. If they were correct, could you explain why in October 1998 there could be as many as 200.000 displaced persons in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I have been trying to tell you that these figures are not accurate. It is not in dispute that there were some displaced persons, and I told you in which areas, which parts of the territory, but the figures are exaggerated. The thing that is in dispute is why these persons were outside their villages. In the area of Drenica, it was the KLA that had control, and they didn't allow people to return to their homes because they had another mission. That mission was to create a humanitarian catastrophe. In other areas it was different. In my area, people did return to their homes. In Eastern Kosovo, there was not a single person outside their home. In the area of Podujevo, same thing. So the only critical area was Drenica, which was under complete control of the KLA. The territory under the control of the state authorities had no displaced persons. Everybody had returned to their homes. In territories under KLA control, the population was being kept outside their homes, and that's the way they spent the winter, but all of that was done with a particular goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, I appreciate it's difficult to answer a hypothetical question when you obviously feel so strongly that the factual position you're stating is accurate, but what we're talking about here are not statistics derived from the United States. They're not statistics derived from Germany. They're statistics provided by the United Nations, and according to Mr. Nice's recollection, confirmed by Mr. Primakov when he was here. But beyond what you've said, you can't help me any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said everything I could tell you about my area of responsibility. I just asked Mr. Nice if a single state authority of my country had participated in the collection of this data. It is obvious that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the report that we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- on the ELMO, does it say what criterion was used to determine a displaced person?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, just to conclude the debate from my point of view, that may be the very -- the most valid point you've made here on this subject, Mr. Delic, that your state didn't collect the data, and indeed the other states that you don't trust didn't collect the data. We're talking about data that were assembled apparently independently, and that's why I'm so interested in it, because I appreciate that one may not give as much weight to evidence presented from someone who has an axe to grind in the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I could help by asking Mr. -- asking Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, please. I did not say -- or maybe you did not understand my evidence correctly. I just asked whether those independent teams of the United Nations included representatives of any state authority of my country. Perhaps a non-governmental organisation, or maybe the Red Cross, but from my country. That was the only thing I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Prendergast would be good enough to put the first page of this exhibit on the overhead projector, we may get some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a letter dated the 5th of February, 2002, to Mr. Blewitt, the then deputy prosecutor. It comes from Neill Wright whose materials are part of the evidence in this case, and I'll read slowly to you the relevant paragraphs, Mr. Delic. "Your office has been asked to explain -- has asked for my assistance to explain the data published ... in 1999 ..." Next paragraph: "As part of its mandate to protect and coordinate the delivery of humanitarian aid to persons affected by the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, UNHCR has been responsible to collect from time to time data about the number and condition of displaced persons and refugees so affected. Ordinarily, UNHCR publishes this data." He then deals with his own position. In the next paragraph after that, he says this: "As in its operations worldwide, UNHCR relied on a variety of sources to compile statistical data linked to the Kosovo refugee crisis. In addition to the data collected by the UNHCR field staff, we also used, after reviewing it for reliability and accuracy, information obtained from local government officials, the Red Cross and non-governmental organisations in the area." Next paragraph you may want me to read, and I do: "It should be understood that some of the data relating to refugees or displaced persons quoted by UNHCR is based on estimates, and not actual head counts." But he then goes on to deal with not internal displacements but refugees. So that's his explanation. Field officers, Red Cross, non-governmental organisations, but also local government officials. Now, can you help us further with His Honour Judge Bonomy's question, if it be the case that the figures were --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Some things are becoming clearer to me now. While on the ground, I toured Albanian villages as well, because there were few Serbian villages anyway. There was not a single Albanian house where I didn't see from five to 20 tons of flour and five to 20 big oil jerrycans of 20 to 200 litres. Now, I would like you to tell me what is the criterion for adequate supplies of these staples per person, because I couldn't understand at the time why Albanian houses held such large quantities of flour. Whereas earlier they used to buy it for their own money, at that time they were getting it from the United Nations in the form of aid. Large amounts were spent on aid. Everybody who was in Kosovo was able to see that while refugees were going to Albania, in addition to their own tractors they also had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you really telling us, just so we can understand it, that being confronted by United Nations statistics explains to you something that had been puzzling you since 1998? Is that what you're saying? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family, too, is now refugeed in Serbia, and I know what is the ration received every month by every displaced persons. What Albanian families received in their villages at the time were humungous quantities of food, and that is why I believe that this number is exaggerated. And I'm telling you again, in my area of responsibility, which was very large, there were no refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You connect the excessive provision or the generous provision of aid by the United Nations to corrupted United Nations figures of statistics. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. You sometimes use strange language. Even in this text that you read, it says that the statistics are based on estimates, not actual head counts, which means that somebody reported that a certain number of refugees existed in a certain area, and based on that estimate aid was allocated to the area in question. The aid also benefited the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I'm going to be able to take that any further in the time available, and unless the Court has questions on it I have one more question of the witness at this stage on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Expecting as you did aggression, as you describe it, from NATO, you must have expected either refugees or an increase in the existing numbers of displaced persons and refugees. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every war, regardless of where it's going on, there are refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Given the army's duty as one of the authorised bodies of power and so on, what plans were made to deal with the refugees that you would inevitably have been expected to be caused by a NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other authorities primarily in charge of the refugees. The job of the army is to defend the country, but there are other institutions in the country, starting with local self-administrations through humanitarian organisations and other to deal with refugees. The task of the army is primarily to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I right to this extent: You personally, for example, expected there to be refugees?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I expected refugees, but I did not expect those refugees to head towards Albania. That part of this scenario was not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look briefly at tab 252, you'll find that it's the second of the two extracts from security reports. One of several, but certainly another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to raise again the various issues we've raised on admissibility and so on of this document, but simply to note that it runs between the 16th of December and the 15th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is an extract again, is it not, Mr. Delic? It's an extract, isn't it, selected by someone?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we've seen, and I don't need to go through it again -- we saw in the previous example of an intelligence report like this that the radio operators picked up everything, including the movements of Serb forces, police forces, things like that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I right that the radio operators who prepare reports like this are able to rely on incoming signals, not just from KLA people but also from police forces, VJ forces in their area of observation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The equipment does not distinguish between various signals. It just monitors everything on the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... material is therefore written down. Now, we've seen yesterday in the little visual aid we looked at how near Racak is to your area of operation, but one way or another can we be satisfied that material of the type provided in this intelligence extract must have been prepared covering the events at Racak? The police would have been sending signals, the army would have been sending signals. The intelligence listeners would have recorded it, so there must be a similar document somewhere dealing with Racak, mustn't there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if such a document exists I am not aware of it. However, when reports are being prepared there is a certain system to them, a format. There is an item dealing with terrorist forces, and that's one section. There is another section dealing with the forces of Albania, then a separate section dealing with communications within our army. That is the entire document, and we see here only one segment dealing with terrorist communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. I have an objection to make, Mr. Robinson, to the fact that Mr. Nice, in examining the witness, presented an observation or claim which leads the witness to misunderstand the question, to lead him astray. Mr. Nice claimed that this matter with respect to the refugees was confirmed by the former Prime Minister of the Russian Federation, Yevgeny Primakov, and this claim was taken up by Mr. Bonomy and also asked a question following on from that, and that is just not correct or accurate. On page 3361 of the transcript from the testimony of Premier Primakov in November 2004 - the page number was 33961 - he quotes a report from the UN Secretary-General and says the following: "'According to the UNHCR [In English] estimates, there could be up to 50.000 displaced people in Kosovo who have been forced from their homes into the woods and mountains.' "Are those figures that you were able then and are you able now to accept?" [Interpretation] The answer that Mr. Primakov gave is this: "I simply don't know. [In English] If that's the report of the Secretary-General, and if he's quoting some figures, then they must be based on the information that was available to him. But the question of whether I agree with each of these figures or not is out of place -" out of place - "because it is absolutely not within my competence as a witness to confirm or not to confirm something that is said by the Secretary-General in his own report." [Interpretation] Therefore, I should like to ask you to make this kind of manipulation impossible, not to allow it, and it is something that Mr. Nice resorts to fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'd like to have confirmed is whether Mr. Nice did put a question to the witness on the basis that the UNHCR figures had been -- had in fact been confirmed by Mr. Primakov.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did. I think I was rather more cautious in the way I expressed it because I knew that it was documents we were putting in, I didn't have them to hand, through Mr. Primakov which were documents that went to the United Nations and were participated in by the Russians, and that's the reason I put them in through him, and that was certainly what I was attempting to explain in short form and then acting from memory. I have the documents here which we can -- or some of them which we can find at tab 16 of Exhibit 795, which is, for example, a report of the United Nations Security Council prepared pursuant to Resolution 1160, and it's this sort of document that I had in mind which refers to figures of displacements of 20.000 people in October 1998, 200.000 -- a reference to the UNHCR's estimates of 200.000 in Kosovo, 80.000 in neighbouring countries, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the point was put this way: "We had a Prosecution -- a Defence witness, Primakov -- I haven't got the exhibit to hand, we'll find it -- the Russian senior politician who prepared -- who was party to reports that were tendered at the United Nations, showing very large numbers of Albanians displaced in the second half of 1998." So that suggests he was party to the preparation of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Party, but as a senior politician. I wasn't suggesting that he was a statistician nor was it ever my intention to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be I also read too much into your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, now that the matter has been clarified and the witness has heard the answer that was given to Mr. Nice when he cross-examined the witness, would the witness want to say anything in relation to the answer that he just gave? I would give you an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is this: The assertions made by Mr. Nice did mislead me, and I consider that that is improper. I stand by what I said, that the number of refugees was much, much smaller and that the number of refugees was greatest in territory under KLA control, which is the Drenica area, and that on the territory controlled by our own forces everything was done to have the people return to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just on that last point, the report that I've just been reading out, you see, which is contemporary to this extent, it's dated the 3rd of October 1998, says of Drenica the following: "These operations --" it speaks of the forces intensifying their operations in an offensive in Drenica and it says, "These operations have reportedly resulted in the displacement of some 20.000 additional people." Does that fit with your recollect of events at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drenica area is outside my area of responsibility. As far as the October period that you mention is concerned, the combat operations had ceased by then, because that was the time, between the 8th and 12th of October, when an agreement was reached about the Verification Mission, and that can be checked out in their reports. So at that time there were -- there was no fighting on any large scale at all except for sporadic incidents, attacks on roads, ambushes, and the laying of mines, that kind of thing. And I've already said -- I said in the previous days that the plan against the terrorist operation, which had five stages, began in July or, rather, the end of July and the beginning of August, and it ended at the end of September, and by the end of September the main terrorist bands had been crushed, and after that control was established on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Drenica was a special area, a separate region which, due to the configuration of the terrain and because of the large number of terrorist groups there that were located, that area was always problematic from the aspects of territory control. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does 20.000 sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up to 20.000 would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Primakov was a member of something called the Contact Group whose very duty it was to monitor what was happening in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. All I know is that he was a member of that Contact Group. But anything else related to Mr. Primakov is not a question you should be asking me. I quite simply don't know his duties and assignments and what he did in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask, Your Honours, any further questions about volume -- at least, I don't think I am, about volume 4, but you may want to keep it because it covers the period about which I'm going to ask questions and the witness may want to refer us to one or two entries in it. I'm going to refer to this document. I'm not particularly asking it to be exhibited, but knowing the problems on looking back at proceedings when documents are not identified, might it be sensible to give it an identification -- a marked for identification reference so that whenever I refer to it I can use that reference and if we re-read the transcript we'll know what I'm talking about, but it's up to the Court entirely. If you're happy with aide-memoire, I'm -- I'll try and use a standard term, and we'll use the term "aide-memoire" if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the aide-memoire, if you'd be so good, north-east of your marked area of responsibility --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any basis at all for Mr. Nice to introduce a document of this kind which can only be his own personal aide-memoire. It's not a document of any kind. It can just be his own aide-memoire but has nothing to do with the document. He can construct a million such similar documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why we're calling that an aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the north-east sector of the thing shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure why he wouldn't be able to use it, Mr. Milosevic. I don't understand the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I might well produce more of these if they're useful. We've already produced some, Mr. Saxon reminds me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice, in the cross-examination, can pose specific questions to the witness, just as I did, with respect to I think about some 20 witnesses whose statements General Delic challenged, beginning with Ashdown right down to those two protected witnesses of his, always concrete. However, this kind of list of all possible documents, all and sundry, cannot be placed before the witness because that would require an enormous amount of work on the part of the witness for him to be able to grasp the contents of the testimonies, to read the transcripts and to find responses to what is being brought up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe the accused can be made to understand what we're doing and I can get on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the witness need to have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He doesn't need to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm happy to have my copy, and if Mr. Milosevic doesn't want the witness to have one, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's simply a document to assist the witness and the Chamber in understanding the evidence. I don't think Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there is any sinister purpose behind it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really -- this document, this piece of paper doesn't really mean anything to me. I can keep it here beside me but it is of no importance as far as I'm concerned. But while we're on the matter, Mr. President, at the end of business today -- yesterday, you know that I asked for a point to be pinpointed with respect to Mr. Ashdown's position and location, and I did my homework related to Suva Reka. So if you want me to present this to you now or at the end of business today, I would like to tell you what I was able to do with respect to Mr. Ashdown's territory from the Suva Reka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that later, General, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, then, go to the question I was asking a long time ago. Javor and Luznica, were they in your area of responsibility? For those looking at the aide-memoire, north-eastern section, north-eastern perimeter. Were they in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to look at the document. What period are you referring to? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: January 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time they were under the responsibility of 223rd Mechanised Brigade -- 243rd Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware the following reported in "As Seen, As Told" at page 354 in the English version, that on the 14th of January, there was reported tank, mortar, and heavy machine-gun and small-arms fire near those villages but that the OSCE were denied access to the area? Do you know anything about that? Just yes or no, and if you say no, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that that was in the area of the -- of responsibility of another unit. No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's then now go, for those looking at the aide-memoire, further south to Jeskovo, February 1999. Remember the position about saying anything that would identify the witness K32. K32 has told us that in February 1999, there were a large number of soldiers and policemen surrounding Jeskovo and that he saw you in the village. Is he right about that, or may he be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before the witness answers that, the aide-memoire does not refer to that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour is quite right. It refers to K41. There's another reference that should be in there. The aide-memoire is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the question is as intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is as intended, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been difficult to try and get all references in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he or may he be right about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we going to refer to the tabs --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you wish to.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from my exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish to, take us to it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's look at the map. It is the 11th -- just let me make sure of the date. Tab 324.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That takes us, therefore, to volume 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while we are locating the document, the witness yesterday said that K32 had been three kilometres away from him. Is it referring to another place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's another incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was the incident of the shelling of the house, if Your Honour remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it wasn't here. And I'll point you to it in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, have you found the map? Which is the tab you want us to look at?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're talking about Jeskovo, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that is tab 324. Tab 325 is the map, and tab 326 is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, the date may have been uncertain in the mind of the witness, so do you say that the only time that it could have been in Jeskovo was in March? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I was in command of that unit and I was in Jeskovo. So that was on the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if it's the 11th of March rather than an uncertain February, is it the case that the witness K32, although you're not going to say anything to identify him here in Court you say you know or you know who it is, is it possible that he saw you in the village?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not possible, and I've already explained why once. He could have seen me in the evening, after the end of the operations when the unit was gathering its forces up in Zagradska, the Zagradska area, and all the units went back to the Prizren barracks, prepared to go back. And all the units rallied round that point who had taken -- which had taken part. So I'm indicating where the witness was and where I was. This is the axis. This is the general direction of the unit of that particular witness, and he moved along in this direction, took this route, and the collection point was in the Zagradska area. I was here, and on the map you can see the mark denoting my command post. So I moved along towards the village of Jeskovo and through the village of Jeskovo directly and took the road back before it became dark to the Zagradska area where the whole unit amassed. And in that region, we had the observers from the Verification Mission, and on the 12th they did an on-site investigation in the village together with the MUP members, the MUP team. And I've already told you that the commander wrote about this event, the commander of the unit, of the Siptar 125th Brigade, the Siptar terrorist forces, and his name was Zafir Berisha, the commander, and he writes this on page 299 in his book "The Road to Freedom."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have that as an exhibit, and let me just complete what I want to raise with you by way of Prosecution evidence. The other witness, K41, who speaks of similar, not identical number of soldiers but a large number, 700, he says, in positions near Jeskovo with police units, says that you were overheard to say that, "We should not -" that is the soldiers - "let a single person remain alive." That's what's been given in evidence. True or false or a misunderstanding or what?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have told you a number of times that I am a Serb officer and a Serb officer would never be able to say anything like that, especially not by myself. That is a pure fabrication on the part of the soldier, and it didn't only come from his mouth, it wasn't uttered only from his mouth. He was prepared to say something like that, things along those lines, and I've already said that that soldier was three kilometres away from that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you want to make that assertion. Prepared by whom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, you coach your witnesses, prepare them, and the preparations and coaching went on in Kosovo and in other places. Your witness was a protected witness, and in my state he is on the wanted list. There is a warrant out for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you want to make that sort of assertion about coaching witnesses, do you want to identify the material upon which you rely to make such an assertion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I want to do is to tell you this: Your witness is telling an absolute untruth, and there is proof to back that up, to back up the fact that he is giving false information to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is a separate matter and one that we can easily deal with, but what's the basis for saying that the witnesses are coached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness K41, after having committed a crime in my country, fled. He escaped. He was in the -- and went to K32 and hid there for several months in K32's home. And in the same kitchen where K32 was prepared is where K41 was prepared or coached as well. And the motive of -- for his testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, your statement was "Mr. Nice, you coach your witnesses." Now, what's the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because the point you do make, the point you try to make about the witnesses getting their heads together is a perfectly valid point, and it gets clouded when you make unfounded allegations. So it would be helpful if you restrained yourself on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, it may well be that the same investigator took both witness statements. That -- I think it's probably the case. But if you now want to suggest that to your knowledge an investigator coached witnesses, please will you tell me on what you base that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said everything I wanted to say linked to that particular witness and to connect it to his testimony. I don't want to claim even that your investigators are preparing witnesses in -- with ill intention, but there are structures which are -- which prepare witnesses, coach witnesses, and K32 was prepared for testimony in Pec. I'm telling you now he was prepared in Pec, and this was done by certain individuals, by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you must understand - we of course have the advantage of the transcript - that your last answers on this are completely inconsistent. You were initially prepared to challenge either me or by inference those working for me as having coached witnesses. You've now withdrawn it and come with a different account which would never have justified making the allegation against the Prosecution and said it was done by Albanians. Mr. Delic, those two answers simply cannot co-exist honestly, can they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already apologised to you, Mr. Nice, because very often -- but very often you do try and put words into my mouth, some of your words into my mouth. So I have said what I said in connection to those two witnesses. I said it's -- over the past two days, and if we want to discuss those witnesses we can do so on the basis of evidence and proof. So I have evidence and proof about what they claim and we could go through those documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say I put words into your mouth. Just one minute. First of all, is that the sort of reply to my questions that anyone has suggested to you you should make?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me very unclear questions. I was irritated by the fact that you kept insisting on certain things, and I'm certainly not claiming that you personally are preparing witnesses, especially not witnesses of this kind, of this type who lie in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you gave the answer you did, the question that led to it was my setting out basically the simple evidence that K41 had given, namely to the effect that you had said, "Don't let a single person remain alive," and I said, "Is that true or false or a misunderstanding or what?" Now, you're now saying that that question put words into your mouth. It didn't put words into your mouth; it asked you a question, Mr. Delic. I want to know why in answer to such a question you came back with the assertion that he'd been prepared and coached.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, throughout the past few days during your cross-examination, you've been using different methods and different approaches to questions and very often improperly so, even perfidiously. You've posed your questions in that way very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You must press on with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you need to restrain yourself. The use of the word "perfidiously" is unfortunate. Mr. Nice is an officer of the Court, and he must operate within the rules and procedures of the Court, and also importantly within the certain ethical constraints which apply to him, and so that was why he reacted as he did when you said he coached witnesses. That's a serious allegation. And to say that he's putting questions perfidiously is another -- another matter that goes to his professionalism. So I have to ask you to restrain yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Delic, every time in the course of the last few days that you've tried to raise an issue about the form of a question, I've taken you back to the precise words, which is something we can do with the transcript. And there are two points that I'm going to make to you. The first is that these reactions of yours actually reveal that you're caught and that you're looking for a way out when you know you have no honest way out, and that's why you resort to this line of attack on me or the investigators or anybody else. Now, that's the suggestion. Do you want to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Once we get the answer to this, Mr. Nice, I'd like you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've put it well, Mr. Nice. That is your assertion. I can only smile at your assertion. I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And moving on as I do, I nevertheless want to revert to -- I may do. Let me just read my question. I'll press on. The evidence given by these two witnesses which has you instructing that no person should be left alive is true, isn't it, and that's why you've reacted in the way you have.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I've said it: That is your opinion, and that is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within the papers that you've brought to this Court, which are the contemporaneous documents that can assist us as to what actually happened? Is it just document 324 or are there any other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just raise a matter here? What date are we dealing with? The Prosecution witness is asserting February. The Defence witness says this is March I'm dealing with and it's the 11th and 12th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. March. Is the Prosecution changing their case that it's not February and it is March or are they saying that it happened in February? Let's be precise, otherwise we're going to be meandering for ages and getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The characterisation is quite inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me. The Judges will say whether my characterisations are inappropriate and we don't need any insulting in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what date are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I made it clear that it was an uncertain February, on the record, and I made it clear to the witness that if there was only the one occasion when they were in this place and it was March and he could, as it were, show that, then that may very well be the incident to which the witness is referring who didn't have the advantage of contemporaneous records of any kind to date it. The witness went on, as the Court will recall, to identify an event and indeed to accept the presence in the area of one of the witnesses, and I've been working on the basis that that is the incident that the witnesses were referring to and that the present witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It makes a difference as to whether it's February or March, whether it can be accepted, whether the witness was in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to me that the Prosecution are now relying on the date that the general says his brigade was there. But am I right in thinking that this incident is not actually referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour is perfectly right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which struck me as peculiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the general allegations, it's there and it's very serious so far as this witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if I may, Mr. Delic, apart from this particular document, 324, do we have any other contemporaneous documents, your log or anything of that kind, that can be produced from your briefcase that will cover this incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the most relevant evidence is here in tabs 324, 325, and 326. So if your witness is talking about February, then I can only say that in February, in that territory, nothing was going on, and my unit was not there in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in March, following the incident described in your tab 324, were any prisoners taken? You might want to look at 8.1. I don't know if that helps us. 324, paragraph 8.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 324 is an order, as I understand it, and 326 is the analysis that follows the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we should look at 326 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 325 is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 326, as His Honour suggests, it may be the report. Is that the document we should be looking at?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can have a look at all three documents parallelly. They were all written at the same time, and they're all relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were any prisoners taken? Look at the top of -- in English, the top of page 2 of the document of the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here exactly in the document whether there were any prisoners or not, that is to say in tab 326.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says no prisoners were taken.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were nine fatalities, there were no prisoners, and there were three wounded members of our own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But no losses, no fatalities in your forces.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this loss of nine with no prisoners consistent with your having given an order that no person there should be left alive?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your insinuations. I never issued such an order, not in that occasion or ever, on any other occasion. Here in the village of Jeskovo there was a special unit of the 125th Brigade, a special unit in black uniforms. Throughout the fighting that went on, they kept saying, "Allahu Akbar," "Allah is great," in translation. That meant that fighters like that never surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the bottom of English page 2, and for you the third paragraph on the second page, please, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I just ask the witness. The group that you were encircling, what was its strength? How many constituted the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we believe that no one from that group got out of the encirclement. Our assessment was that there were between 25 and 30 of them. However, since this group had the task to mobilise the population in the surrounding area, part of the group was probably staying in other villages, like Zur or some other village in the area. Also, there is reference here to our own estimate regarding the strength of that group. However, at that moment we came across only nine of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If nine was killed, no one was captured, that would have left about 20 or 21 unaccounted for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were members who were not encircled on that day. They were elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, yes. So the nine who were killed represented the totality of the number that you were -- that you were encircling at that time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you've told us you were expecting 30. In his evidence, a long time ago now, K41 said that he saw no return fire but it was expected, he believed, a total of 30 was killed. He didn't have access to contemporaneous records. I would suggest to you that the nine that were killed in the expectation of there being 30 were killed because you gave this order that no one should be left alive.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is a point of your own that is totally unfounded. I would just like to get a document out now to show what the OSCE says about that and what the commander of the Siptar forces says about that. I've already showed it once here. I'll have to look for it during the break, because right now I can't find it. However, if you remember, I have already presented it to you. Even the names of these people are mentioned there. The OSCE gave its own report in terms of verifying that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would be good enough to go with me, as I suggested, to the second page of document tab 326, noting on the way that you had six tanks present, double barrelled anti-aircraft guns, we see that your ammunition is at the bottom of the page, used amounted to 1.656 7.62 millimetre bullets for an automatic rifle, 600 7.62 millimetre bullets for an M-84 machine-gun; is that right? Then some 120-millimetre shells. Is it 18? I think that's the way one reads it. 13 82-millimetre shells, 16 90-millimetre shells, 19 100-millimetre bullets, seven impact rifle grenades, seven M-75 fragmentation hand grenades. And you make the point, and you may want to reflect on this, it may or may not help you, I'm not sure, that the command -- this is the top of page 3, please,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRENDERGAST
utterances.text: "The command of the selected forces was achieved through a joint command of the MUP and VJ forces ..." Now, is that quantity of weaponry consistent with an effort to take prisoners if possible and to kill only if necessary or is that consistent with an all-out assault on this place at any cost?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we had, there was a special KLA unit there, the best trained, the best equipped terrorists, who were ready to fight to the bitter end. Surrender was not an option for them. These men who were in black uniforms, who trained together with Mujahedin, I already said that throughout the fighting "Allahu Akbar" was the only thing heard from their ranks. No one ever surrendered. They all died from infantry fire. Nobody died from our artillery fire. I found it. May I put this on the overhead projector, please? There are only three sentences that the commander of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read it slowly. I hope it will be interpreted. "On the 15th of March, I heard quite a bit of touching information. I heard of the heroic death of many comrades, heroes who had proven themselves earlier on. These were the following heroes: Hunjan Rajepi [phoen], Beskim Suka [phoen], Hajdra Sala [phoen], Feri Susurri [phoen], Tahir Gashi, Skender Latifi, Umerdin Cengaj [phoen], Ajadinje Zahiri [phoen] and Hamed [phoen] Thaci. Those are soldiers of the special unit of the 125th Brigade of the operation zone of Pastrik and this was truly a great loss because the fighting went on at a distance between 15 and 20 metres." Now let me show you what the OSCE wrote, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document you were looking at was? Just tell us so that we know.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I just read out is from the -- from the book of the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 125th Brigade, Zafir Berisha. The book is called "The Road to Freedom," and it's on page 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the OSCE document that you are now going to read from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is from the fund, from the Humanitarian Law Fund, "As Seen, As Told," but it pertains to the perceptions of the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you've obviously got -- have you got the whole of that document with you, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but he's got it in B/C/S, which I was looking, actually, for this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we saw that on the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the B/C/S version of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I saw that you had that book the other day. You held it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not in the B/C/S version, you see. Go on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope somebody is going to translate what I'm going to read out, because I do not have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, please speak slowly, more slowly, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the beginning of March fighting broke out around Hoca Zagradska to the south-west of Prizren. Around 200 persons left on the -- left the village on the 11th of March and went to the north towards Prizren but the police stopped them. During the ceasefire, the displaced persons returned to their village, but the fighting was renewed and about 100 persons left Hoca Zagradska again and went north. "During the operations of the security forces on the 11th of March, the villagers of Jeskovo, that is further into the mountains to the south-east of Hoca Zagradska, left their homes and returned a few hours later. After heavy bombing by the combined Serb forces that used tanks and armoured carriers, artillery and mortars, some houses were in flames. It has been reported further that the KLA responded to these attacks with an attack in the area of Zociste, near the road between Suva Reka and Orahovac in the Orahovac municipality, using mortars and heavy machine-guns. During most of these operations the OSCE-KVM did not have any access to the region. The Regional Centre of the OSCE and the KVM in Prizren commented on the situation, saying that the KLA had infiltrated into Jeskovo, a previously abandoned village, about a week before that. The inhabitants of Hoca Zagradska informed the OSCE-KVM about their concerns and the KLA withdrew. The OSCE-KVM informed the KLA that the local population and the security forces considered their presence in this area to be a provocation. In addition to all of that, the OSCE-KVM in Prizren recorded that the Serb forces during this fighting limited fighting to Jeskovo only, to the south of Prizren. Other villages had been occupied but not damaged. "On the 12th of March, the police called the OSCE-KVM teams to visit Jeskovo, the village that was in the focus of the police operation of the 11th of March. The verifiers saw the bodies of seven armed men in black uniforms of the KLA. According to statements made by the police, they were killed by fire from sidearms during the security operation. Teams could not establish whether the members of the KLA were killed in places --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have the text back on because it was way too fast. The bottom of the page, please, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters are asking to see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The teams could not establish whether the members of the KLA were killed in places where they were lying. The verifiers were also showed a small calibre mortar with ammunition prepared for use --" and then the text goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 340 on the English version. There's only one page difference. Everything you've told us, Mr. Delic, including the expectation that these people would fight to the death, does that fit with your giving the order that everybody should be killed, which is what the witness says?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I said a few moments ago that you are putting some of your words into my mouth. I never said and not a single army officer would have said that all people should be killed. Please never repeat that again. That was not my order. That is a lie uttered by your witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the top of page 3 of the document that you drew to our attention, and indeed have in mind what the OSCE said about the presence of the police as one source, you referred to this as being through a joint command of the MUP and VJ forces. Well, now, this is a different use of the words "joint command" from the one we'd been looking at earlier, but how did it operate?
