Who ran things when you had a joint operation like this under a joint command or through a joint command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to deny what you're saying straight away, because what you're saying does not correspond to reality. There was no Joint Command. When it says that there is singleness of command, that means that the commander of the police forces was next to me, that he and I were in one place, that I commanded my forces and that he commanded his forces. And I was there. You were not there, and you don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... trying to in a sense help you, but you react as you do. I said that the use of the words "joint command" here is different maybe from the other sense. Let's go to the original text, if you'd be so good, please. Lay it on the overhead projector and just read out the words that refer to joint command and see how it comes out in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that will be, if you lay the Serbian text on the overhead projector, please, Mr. Prendergast, then above "Conclusions" it's one, two, three -- it's just about a third of the way down the page, where it says -- begins with the word "Komandovanje," then something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So perhaps you'd just read that out for us, please, Mr. Delic, the single sentence that begins with "Command," is it? I'm not sure. We can see exactly how the words are used. There we are. Can you just read that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commanding of the envisaged forces was unified by the Joint Command of the forces of MUP and the VJ and was safe and timely."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So can you just help us, because we may -- none of us have military experience, or we may -- or I know some of us have military experience. In circumstances of such danger, do you not need a single person to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a military professional, I believe that in all such situations it would be a good idea, but in order for that to happen certain decisions need to be made. Thus there is an Article 16, an Article 17 in the law on defence that envisages the possibility, but only in a state of war, of that kind, but it is provided for only as a possibility. And because that is so, appropriate decisions or directives have to be adopted for it to happen on the ground. This was happening in March, and the sentence reads as I read it, and it implied that the commander of the MUP forces and I should be in the same place together, as we were on a number of occasions earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. May I just have sight of either the extract of the B/C/S version of "As Seen, As Told" or the whole copy of it if you've got the whole copy there, please, just for one reason? I'll hand it become almost immediately. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- can I clarify the translation of this document. It was translated as this: "Command of the envisaged forces was unified," while the transcript said -- no, no, our document says "was achieved." Is there any nuance, difference of nuances in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's "command of the envisaged forces was unified" as opposed to "command of the selected forces was achieved." I think that's the divergence. Maybe, as so often, it depends on the interpreter. And, Your Honours, just to clarify something that was concerning Mr. Kay and that explained why I allowed for different dates for the incident in the evidence of the witnesses, our researchers remind us that K41 spoke of the incident in February, K32 spoke of it being in March. So that they gave different periods in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One last question on this topic and I'm going to move on. Apart from this document that you've shown to us, Mr. Delic, these two documents, are there any other documents that you've got with you, logbooks, daily records, intelligence reports, et cetera, et cetera, that cover this event?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have said this a couple of times before: A war diary is kept only during the war. This was not wartime. There is an operations log which is kept every day by the duty operations officer. That operations log exists. I don't have it with me but it exists in Belgrade. I searched for it in the archives unsuccessfully, but I failed to find it only because our archives are bogged down by the huge number of these documents, but I will continue looking for it anyway because I need it myself. There is documentation to confirm that it has been transmitted to the archives, but in the past two years I have not been successful in finding it. It exists, therefore. But it is not so detailed as the reports are. It just says that on that day the unit was engaged on such-and-such an axis, and if there were any losses, the losses are identified and named as well as those who were wounded, in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would radio traffic have been logged by a radio operator at headquarters listening in to what was being said?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the duty operations officer has equipment monitoring what is going on on the ground, and if there is anything relevant, he reports it to me, but he cannot monitor several different waves at the same time. He can only follow traffic on one airwave that was designed -- designated by the command. He takes notes as instructed, and he executes my orders or invites other commanding officers as necessary. As far as monitoring of radio traffic is concerned, that is something that could only be done by one unit, the company for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic operations, but normally there is all kind of traffic on the air, communications among terrorists, among MUP forces, and among army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, is there any circumstance in which in your view it would be justified for an officer such as yourself to have given the order which the Prosecution says that you gave to your forces to ensure that no one was left alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the rules of service binds all soldiers from private to the highest ranking commander to execute each and every order of their superior except for orders which would constitute a crime. So if I should ever have ordered civilians to be killed, which is completely nonsensical, no soldier and no officer would have carried that order out because they are equally bound by the law, as I was. And the rule says that if they, nevertheless, receive such an order, they should report it to the superior commander, bypassing the immediate level from which they got the order. There is another mechanism in place, another line, another chain of command, namely the security organs, which independently follow all the developments in the unit. We had a security organ in our unit as well. They are not reporting to me. They report along their own chain of command. Their only duty to me is to bring to my attention incidents in the unit, if any, to provide me with certain information -- something is going on with the headphones. They also have the duties. They work on combatting crime. They have the duty to report to me any data regarding possible crimes in the unit, but they are linked, in terms of chain of command, to their own superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're saying, then, that you cannot conceive of any situation in which you could have given such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am prepared to sign my own hundred year sentence to imprisonment if I ever uttered such an order. That is an order that could not cross the mind of a professional officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty for me with the answer, which I must say I had expected to be much simpler, was that it appeared to be confined to an order relating to civilians and the question wasn't. The question was whether you could ever conceive of a situation where you would give the order which the Prosecution claim you did, and that's a much wider question, I think, than the one you've answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, that's inconceivable and impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why would that be? Why would that be now if you're tracking not civilians but insurgents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you can fight an enemy as long as they are holding weapons. As early as in the first year of the military academy and then throughout my military training, I was taught Geneva Conventions. From the moment when somebody lays down their weapon, he is no longer considered as a soldier, and you're not allowed to fight him. He is a prisoner, and it is very precisely envisaged and stipulated what you may do with a prisoner. We have gone through various tabs here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We observed from the passage of the Humanitarian Law Fund's book, as you describe it, "As Seen, As Told," that there was no certainty that the bodies had died where they were found. There is another record which I'm just sending for, but I know what it says - at least I'm pretty sure I know what it says - and I'll read it to you and we'll then get it for the overhead projector. The blue book, which was a contemporaneous record, said the following: "Yesterday's fighting south of Prizren appears to have subsided." The group, RC1, as it's called, "was invited by the MUP to investigate the results of that fighting." This is an entry for the 13th of March. "Seven dead KLA were found on the outskirts north of Jeskovo and had apparently died from small-arms fire. All were dressed in black overalls with an AK weapon near each body." Now, thus far, does that accord with your account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that tallies with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The on-site investigation was done on the 12th. As for the mission, they insisted that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there. I want to read you the rest of the entry. If I may. The book is coming down. Because it's said -- it went on to say the following: "One of the bodies had an entry bullet wound in the centre of the forehead with an apparent attempt to cover the head with foliage. None of the bodies appeared to have died in these positions but had been carefully laid out on their backs with weapons placed nearby. It is believed that the bodies may have been 'imported' from elsewhere." Now, was there any question of the bodies being laid out in positions, with weapons placed nearby, for the mission to view?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. There's no need. The bodies were just retrieved from the brook. The terrorists had tried to escape through a mountain brook where the water was about 50 centimetres deep. It was the time of year when the snow melts. And practically walking on all fours, because you can't swim in that brook, it's too shallow, they tried to leave the village. They ran into an ambush which was about 20 metres away from them, and all of them were hit, all but four -- or, rather, all but two. There were all hit while they were still in the brook. After that, they were carried further on by the water for several metres. One of them stopped at a bend. Some other bodies were carried a bit further away. We just retrieved them from the water and laid them on the grass, and then we continued to look for their weapons. We knew they had automatic rifles. They had an Armbrust, and in the house where they had been located earlier there was a mortar and a large amount of ammunition. So the only manipulation with the bodies was to retrieve them from the brook and lay them on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, in which direction from Jeskovo does the brook flow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It flows -- if you look at this here. If this is Jeskovo, it flows this way, because this is Prizrenska Bistrica river, and the brook flows into the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we need that for the record. Which direction is that? Tell us whether it's north, south, east, or west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That brook flows north-west and into the Bistrica -- Prizrenska Bistrica River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before we rise, Your Honour, just to correct an impression on the date that Mr. Nice gave you concerning the evidence of K32. This is to be found at transcript page 8232, and Mr. Ryneveld gave the date as a leading question, mid-March. He said to the witness: "Let's skip ahead now to about mid-March of 1999, and are you aware, sir, of an offensive of a village known as Jeskovo?" The answer was: "I was not aware of that." And Mr. Ryneveld said, "Well, that's my phrasing. Did something happen with respect to Jeskovo?" So that's how the position in the Prosecution case of the date arose; not from the witness himself. I just put that before you so that we don't let this matter go unnoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kay. We will take the adjournment now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll hear the results of the witness's overnight labour in relation to Lord Ashdown, not now; at about 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've located the extract from the blue book. Just lay it on the overhead projector, please, Mr. Prendergast, so we -- the Chamber will probably remember the general format. It's part of Exhibit 321. I needn't read it again. The Chamber will recall the blue book is put together on a daily basis with various kinds of concentration of information. I'm going to move quickly on through this -- thank you very much. That can come off. If we now go very swiftly on to tab 35 -- sorry, 334.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 334, please, Mr. Delic. I beg your pardon. In fact, I can do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. better than that. Go straight to 336, I think. Sorry again. 338, actually. 338. Save some time. And if we look at 338 - foot of the page, please, Mr. Prendergast - this is a confrontation at Korisa Kabas village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Summary, just in a sentence, what was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only the village of Kabas, and the village of Kabas is located at a distance of one and a half kilometres towards the east from the village of Korisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the end of our page 1, and for you I think it will be on the second page. There's a couple of lines which explain how the operation ended. It says: "During the operation the STS did not drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment, when they changed into civilian clothes and attempted to break through along the Gurit Mahala, where they came across our units in the line of blockade. "During combat operations the inhabitants of Selograzde village, Grejkovce village and Korisa village were seen moving in the direction of Suva Reka and Prizren. "Our estimate of STS losses: "11 killed, no one captured." Now -- and then at the end of the document your equipment: Six tanks, two howitsers, anti-aircraft guns, and so on. It is the real position that by this time operations of this kind where you outgunned the KLA massively were simply take-no-prisoners-kill-everyone operations. Is that the position that you'd achieved by then?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the situation and that was not correct. That is your observation, which is quite inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, at the time that these men were running away in the way that you described the men in other incident running across the stream or through the stream, they had apparently dropped their weapons and changed into civilian clothes but none of them was captured. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're quite simply inventing this. We're talking about this stream. We're saying that everybody saw those people wearing black uniforms, and now you speak about civilian clothing, civilian clothes. They weren't escaping, they hadn't dropped their weapons. They were holding their weapons on them, on their backs or on their breasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm only reading your document, or if not your document whoever's document this one is, and the way we've got it in translation -- it may be the translation, you see, who knows -- but the way it reads is -- it says: "During the operation they didn't drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment, when they changed into civilian clothes and attempted to break through along the Gurit Mahala." It doesn't say -- maybe this is what happened -- it doesn't say they changed into civilian clothes and then, despite trying to look like civilians, carried AK-41s. It says they changed into civilian clothes and tried to run away. So that's why I'm asking you the question. It looks as though they were then ambushed.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the stream, and your linking up the previous event in Jeskovo to this one here. This is something quite different. This is something that happened in the area of Kabas, and Kabas is a mountainous terrain between Suva Reka and Prizren, and in that area there was -- there were no civilians. It's just some dozen houses. And the civilian population mentioned here -- the inhabitants of other villages are mentioned which set along this direction. And if you looked at the estimates of the Siptar forces in our assessment and according to what we saw, it was 30 to 35 men. And if you look further on, you will see that some soldiers on our side were killed, some of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is this your analysis, Mr. Delic, your own analysis? Because it doesn't have a signature on my English copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I was the commander. I have my organs writing for me, but I signed it, which means that I accept it as my own, as my own decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your personal knowledge of this. It is strange the way this reads, actually. You understand the point Mr. Nice is making. He's trying to have it clarified, but it says that while the operation was ongoing the terrorists did not drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment, when they changed into given clothes and attempted to break through along the Gurit Mahala, where they came across our units in the line of blockade." So that could suggest - could suggest - that unarmed terrorists trying to escape were actually killed at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is your opinion, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an interpretation I think that obviously could be made of the document. I am forming and expressing no opinions in the course of this. I'm trying to probe the evidence to see what decisions we should ultimately make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, that means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to make one comment. Mr. Bonomy quoted quite correctly and accurately, and it says quite plainly here attempted to break through, attempted to break through. That's not the same as an attempt at escape. This is armed, intentional break through the lines of our unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say that I find these interventions very unhelpful, because Mr. Delic was there, as you have so often reminded us about witnesses who have been led on your behalf, and he is a gentleman who is perfectly capable of expressing clearly to me what he knows happened without prompting from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, tell us again what happened, what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're dealing with the village of Korisa, and the number of men there was, according to our assessment, 30 to 35, and when we investigated the area where they had been accommodated, that was established. And our forces were able to launch a surprise on them. They were able to set up a blockade along a long stretch. And when our forces were noticed, that's when the fighting started, and this large terrorist group started to pull out towards the north-east, towards the mountains at that time. So one of my units was there. It was the PVO unit, which was supposed to be along the blockade line, and the breakthrough at that point was resorted to because one of my soldiers were killed, one of my soldiers were wounded, and this part of the group that was lacking, about 20 men, that portion managed to break through that part, whereas the rest were killed fighting with the forces or against the forces along the blockade line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did they or some of them change into civilian clothes? At what stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What -- I do know that some of them were wearing civilian clothes. One of my officers at the place where this breakthrough took place and where my soldier Markovic was killed saw a man in civilian clothing at a distance of just 50 metres with the pump action rifle, and at that point in time he didn't know who the man was. And then he noticed this large group which opened fire, and one soldier was killed as a result and another soldier wounded. But when we say the blockade line, that means that not a large force was there, and the distance between the soldiers in that forest was quite great, 15 to 20 metres, maybe even more, the distance apart. So there was some small problems that occurred there after one soldier was killed and another wounded, because part of that force -- they used part of that force to get out of the blockade, of the siege, and part of those men were dressed in civilian clothes. If you take a look at, I think, page 2 -- or, rather, on that same page, perhaps, if we look at the very end of that portion, you will be able to see what was found in the place where these people spent their time. It's the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The English text presents a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it out if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to read anything, read the part beginning "During the operation..." Yes. Read it out so we can have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what he's dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I want you to go back to the beginning: "During the operation the STS did not drop their weapons," so we can have it translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the operation the STS did not drop their weapons or combat equipment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the operation the STS did not drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment when they changed into civilian clothes and attempted to break through along the Gurit Mahala axis, trig point 1613, where they came across our units in the line of blockade. During --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. That's what's in the exhibit tab 338. It doesn't quite accord with the sequence of events that you have given now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to read four more lines, please, a little lower down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the search of the houses in Gurit Mahala, the following was found: 200 12.7-millimetre bullets, about seven kilograms of TNT explosive, three TMM1 anti-tank mines, 20 RB rocket launcher shells, 30 camp beds, three tent equipment sets, 20 sleeping bags, some medical equipment and medicine, about 15 sets of uniforms with KLA insignia, 29 pairs of boots, ten combat rucksacks," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the issue. The issue raised by the Prosecutor is whether when the men were shot and killed, whether they were armed, and the text here in English suggests that they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, those people weren't shot. They died in combat when trying to break through the circle, the encirclement, and a part of them managed to break through the encirclement and took to the mountains, whereas the number mentioned here remained behind on the spot, and at that time one of my soldiers was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were they armed at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them were armed. And as you can see here, no mention is made of the fact where they were any weapons remained. It's just ammunition and explosives that remained on the spot where they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. You're citing the last passage in support of your contention that they were in fact armed, is that so, that weapons and explosives were found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm saying that for the uniforms, for the sake of the uniforms. All that was found, but I'm saying it because of the uniforms. And part them, as I said, was wearing civilian clothes but bearing weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's an issue which the Trial Chamber will have to resolve on the basis of the evidence before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. Incidentally, I just pass over so that the Chamber can have the material in mind, 342. Just quickly look at it, I don't really want to ask anything about it except to draw your attention to it. 342, Stojimirovic writes on the 19th of March an urgent communication suggesting increased security, and he says: "We believe that the goal of the terrorists is to inflict losses on our unit following the events in Jeskovo village and Kabas village."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So described as an event there, Mr. Delic, and the two events linked up. You see?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like this to be corrected for the transcript. You mentioned Ljubisa Stojimirovic, Lieutenant General. He wasn't the person who wrote this brief order that was coded. It was Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Stojiljkovic, my Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next topic, if I can. Can you just go very briefly to 345, tab 345. This is 20th of March. And the second paragraph of the document, which comes from Stojiljkovic, again, relates to: "Above Velika Krusa village individuals were noticed observing the Prizren-Djakovica road." What they did. But then it says this: "In Orahovac we learnt that during the day the local Siptar people left in maybe five or six buses for Macedonia." What was driving them out?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Kosovo and in my country it was clear to one and all that there would be a conflict very shortly, and this is an observation by an officer who was in Orahovac on that particular day and arrived at that knowledge and information. So he is conveying that information to me and informing the corps command. And before that time, too, there were attempts on the part of some people to leave for Macedonia, some Serbs to go to Serbia, and some Albanians also to go to Montenegro. And this then is a presentment that -- because we're already dealing with the 20th here, that's the time when the mission had already left or was leaving the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, so people tried to get away in time, to escape from the war in time, and it was imminent. It was just a question of days when it was going to start. So that's how I understand these people leaving. Nobody forced them out of Orahovac. They left on regular buses and went to Macedonia. But for us it was telling us that something was happening in the territory and something was afoot, looming in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go on to 356. And this is, of course, the document you were asked a lot of questions about in due course. The accused ended his question saying the document's very clear and well laid out, let's not dwell on it, but you'll remember that because of its title, The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, you were asked several questions by the Bench about it. I'm not going to cover that ground again, obviously, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I only have a couple of supplementary points -- not points. I only have a couple of questions to ask. Would you be good enough, please, to go to paragraph 2. This Joint Command document says at paragraph 2: "With reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija --"

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, what tab are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you haven't got there. 356.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 346, or that's what I heard. That's the interpretation I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 356. Different binder. I don't know why. If you've got 356 at paragraph 2, it says: "Assignment: With reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija, the Pristina command is assisting the MUP crushing and destroying STS in the zone of responsibility." So what does "crushing and destroying" mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should -- as this is a specific assignment, we should take a look at a map at this point, with your permission, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are you not able to answer the question without resorting to the map at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer every question without using maps, however, I would like everybody who is following and -- to explain this to you, too, on the ground, what I'm talking about. At this time, and we're dealing with -- let's just take a look at the date. This was written on the 23rd of March, when the mission had already left the country and when we knew that it was just a question of hours when the NATO aggression would be launched. The terrorist forces at that period of time were grouped along individual axes with the task of cutting across the communication lines between Metohija here and Kosovo, and with the task of, in case of an aggression, attack the logistics parts and rear of the units defending the state border. So on the one hand we had an accumulation of forces in the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia, and on the other side we had right behind our backs in the rear strong terrorist groups, and no military commander or military strategist can allow himself to have to fight against two enemies at once, simultaneously, because he would certain -- it would be a battle he would certainly lose. So this assignment was issued, this order was issued, and it said that NATO went ahead with the bombing, we should first break down the terrorist forces, crush the terrorist forces which had amassed in our rear in-depth, and that after that we should concentrate our entire force in defending the state territory, our country. And on the map you can see the deployment of forces; my forces, terrorist forces, and where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's go back to the question I asked you. The words we've got translated are "crushing and destroying." Does that basically mean killing?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crushing means that they should cease to function as a formation, that they should be broken up into smaller groups, if possible to be taken prisoner --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there. I may have missed it at the moment. I'm trying to remind myself of the detail of the document. Does this document deal with prisoners somewhere? Let's have a look for that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite normally there is always a space in a document of this kind which refers to that question, that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just see if we can find it, see what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? It is point 8.2. I was saying if I can be of assistance in this document, it is point 8.2. Yes. It says: "All terrorists captured..." et cetera, "should be taken to places provided for prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Point 8 in our text, Mr. Milosevic, deals with combat security.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I'm looking at a different document. I'm looking at an order by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, we're talking about the corps order. And in point 10 of that order -- in point 10 is where that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says "Interrogate detained persons --" this is on page 5, Your Honours -- "and hand them over to the MUP organs for further processing," the degree to which it deals with prisoners. That's on page 5. So that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the link made, Mr. Delic, between dealing with the KLA, who were behind you, and dealing with the potential threat from the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean where is the link? There is a constant, continuous link. You have one enemy in front of you and one enemy behind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment to see why I thought your answer was particular to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read point 2, if you will, point 2. It is the answer to your question. It's contained in point 2. Paragraph 2, where it says "Task:" Or should I read it out if you would like me to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I can read it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other questions -- three, about this document. You told us yesterday about arming the non-Albanians, and here you're -- the army is in charge of, is it, the armed civilian population who it's now going to deploy to attack the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. It's not the proper observation. That absolutely does not correspond to the actual state. The armed non-Siptar population, it had nothing to do with the army. It was within the system of the units of civilian defence, which were linked to the Ministry of Defence. But when you say in co-action, that is to say if they are in our zone we would directly cooperate with them. Their task was never to attack but was to protect their own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what it says -- that's why I ask you. All I can do, Mr. Delic, is look at the document, you see. And it says: "With reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija, the Pristina Corps or command of Pristina Corps is assisting the MUP." So a simple reading of that sentence would say that the armed non-Siptar population are with the military, assisting the police. I can't make any other construction of it, can you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying, but I was there on the spot. I know which local residents were armed, I know who had which task and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... command themselves?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the army did not command them. There were two elements of the Ministry of Defence; the units of civilian defence and units of civilian protection. These residents belonged to civilian defence, and they had old weapons, weapons that were treated as obsolete in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're not commanded by anybody. If we have time we'll review crimes -- thank you. We'll review crime sites where locals were recognised as perpetrators, and I must suggest to you that this command, this order would suggest that locals were really basically subordinated to or incorporated within the military forces. That's the way it reads. And of course Article 16 of the law on defence says that the army should unite all forces in defence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me refute what you are saying before we move on. First of all, nobody was in command of those units. That's what you said. I don't agree. All those units had each their own responsibility, they had each their own commander, and they were disciplined. They belonged to units of civilian defence. They were not large. They were one squad strong. You know how much -- how strong a squad is; ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a simple question: Who commanded civil defence squads?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian defence forces were under the command of the municipal civil defence staff. So the Chief of Staff of the civilian defence staff was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Next question: Paragraph 4 of this document begins: "I have decided." "Odlucio sam," I think. Who is the "I" who has made the decision?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this document, let's go to the last page, which is unsigned so far as a handwritten signature is concerned, but is typed "the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" is a document of the corps command, and we've finally got there, have we? Joint Command equals the military command.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So to review the position, and this may be contrary to things you said before, the Joint Command is actually the military; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say one thing at the outset: You are speaking much too fast and you are trying to say a great deal. Let me clarify one thing. I have been saying throughout that the Joint Command does not exist in the sense that you are trying to present. There was only one coordinating body there, and that was the Joint Command. The words "I have decided" mean it was decided by the corps commander. Look at tab 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you wish to point out in tab 359?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point. This is my analysis or, rather, my report on the assignment I had received, and you can see where it was sent, the command of the Pristina Corps, no Joint Command. I think that is clearly written here. So I received an order. There is reference to the Joint Command indeed in the order, and I explained why, and I'm not challenging that that is so. But this reference, "Strictly confidential 455/63," that is the number under which it was registered in the Pristina Corps command, in their office. So when the whole thing was over, I did not report about it to the Joint Command. I reported about it to the command of the Pristina Corps, as you can see from tab 359.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mindful of the fact that the witness is to deal with another matter at about half past one, I want to deal with a short point now, a general application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you've got the "As Seen, As Told" document in extract form down there. Is that the only extract you've got or have you got the whole "As Seen, As Told" book with you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the whole book. I took out only the bits --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to tell you. I received that book for a very short time in 2001 or 2002, I don't remember any more, and I copied the part that relates to my municipality, the municipality where I spent some time. That is Prizren. I know what the cover page looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever read the book or try to read it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read most of what has to do with Kosovo and Metohija. And the rest, concerning areas far from my area of responsibility, I did not read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is a book written by a Natasa Kandic, you say, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. This is a book of the Humanitarian Law Foundation, and the main person in that foundation is Mrs. Natasa Kandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's quite right that she's the main person in the organisation. And you're saying that that organisation wrote this book; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the footnotes, I believe she used a lot of data collected by others, because I can see a lot of information comes from Albanians who had left Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, if you'd actually read the book, you'd have discovered that all that Natasa Kandic's organisation had done was to translate it, and that's why the version you've got -- can you lay it on the overhead project, please, just the page that's there. If Mr. Delic picks it up from down there on his right-hand side, or if Mr. Prendergast does, turn over to the next -- second page, Mr. Delic. We can see it, just put the top of it on the overhead projector and we can all see that the book has on the left-hand side the fund, The Humanitarian Law Fund, and then on the right it has "As Seen, As Told." But if you'd actually read the book --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, Mr. Nice. On the right-hand side, it says: "Section 5, Kosovo municipalities and settlements."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now just go with me, please, through these statements that I asked you to describe. Remember I asked you to describe how your colleagues' statements were taken earlier today. Would you go, please, to tab 362. The last paragraph of it. The Court can see it on page 2. This is one of the proffered statements from -- this time from Zlatko Vukovic, and he says this: "I read something about the crimes in the book "As Seen, As Told" published by Humanitarian Law Centre. Since I am disgusted by the author and the fabrication she sets out in the book, I didn't finish reading it." Would you go on, please, to tab 363. At the foot of the page, last paragraph of the statement of Major Janos Sel. Second line: "I read about it in a book published by The Humanitarian Law Centre entitled "Kosovo, As Seen, As Told." 364, please. Captain Elifat Feta's statement, another of the statements that's been offered as exhibits in this case. Last paragraph again: "I first heard about the crime allegedly committed in Bela Crkva in late 2001. I read about it at greater length in Natasa Kandic's book "As Seen, As Told." Paragraph 365, please -- tab 365. Last paragraph of the statement offered of Oliver Ilijevski. Second line: "I later read about it in greater detail in Natasa Kandic's book "Just told them what you saw." And then if we go on, please -- oh, there's another statement from the same chap Vukovic, at 369, where he says he was disgusted by Natasa Kandic, and there are more statements to the same effect. None of the statements that you seek to produce reveal that the readers -- the writers, I beg your pardon, have actually recognised that the book they're quoting was never written or produced by Natasa Kandic, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was simply translated by her, and it's actually a book of research by OSCE. Can you explain that to us in light of what you remember you told us about how statements were prepared?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing peculiar about that. What people wrote here is what they thought, what they meant. They said that it was the first they heard of those crimes, alleged crimes, since the time the indictment was brought, and they first read about them when this book became available, and it became available through the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. In my personal view, this book is very biased. You can read in it only views of one side, and there is all sorts of nonsense here, and I can prove it at any time, as soon as you give me the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that none of you, it would appear, can conceivably have read this book. You may have been provided with excerpts from it but none of you actually read it, because, although it may have -- and that's why I asked you for the front page -- it may well have Natasa Kandic's organisation's logo on the front in some way, and I just don't know to what extent, once you read it, it's clearly -- it's got a foreword by Justice Louise Arbour, it's got a summary, and it's clearly an OSCE document, and were you -- that's one point. And were you aware indeed that the same organisation published another document, called "As Seen, As Told Part 2"? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that one too. However, you just showed a book --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the one. Part 2 deals with crimes perpetrated after the arrival of KFOR, as far as I know, and those crimes include those against Serbs. At least part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are you suggesting then that these persons never read the book at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm drawing to the Court's attention the recurring similar entries in the statements and the fact that if anybody had read the book you could never have thought that it was written other than by the OSCE. That's my point. As to precisely what explains these curious entries, I can go no further than ask the questions I've asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I go back briefly to tab 356. General -- General, could you look at the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let Judge Kwon ask his question first, Mr. Milosevic. Then you can comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 356. Could you read the last paragraph, bullet point 13, so that I can hear the interpretation of B/C/S into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Coordinated action with MUP forces concerning the issue of preparation of combat activities is to be organised before commencement and during the execution of combat operations. With all forces in the course of executing combat operations, command and control is effected by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the region of Pristina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why did you need that last sentence, and what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this is not my order. It's the order that came from Pristina. My order is under one of the following tabs, and my order never mentions the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your answer is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, my answer is not that I don't know. I explained more than once how I understand the term "Joint Command," what it means to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is this last sentence necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, General Pavkovic, who was corps commander then, is here. I as brigade commander have been trying to explain this for days. The Joint Command existed because in 1999, we, the brigade commanders, did not go all together to Pristina to prepare coordination for a certain action. This order was sent down to the MUP, and it was sent down to my unit as well. I received it together with all the other mail, and before that I received a call from the corps commander telling me to prepare my unit for upcoming operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is a separate matter, but I didn't intervene at the time to not interrupt the flow of evidence. In one of your answers you said that your family is now refugeed in Serbia. I'm not clear about that. If you clarify briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my family used to live in Kosovo. After these events, they left Kosovo, and the exact status they have is called something different. They are called temporarily displaced persons, but they have been temporarily displaced since 1999. The entire property we owned in Kosovo was either destroyed or taken over by some Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing: I owe an answer to Mr. Nice, who alleged that my officers did not read the book. That is absolutely not true. The book we read has different cover, different binding than the one I just saw in Mr. Nice's hands, and the book my officers read looks a bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already indicated that so far as I know, but I haven't got a copy, it has somewhere on the front, and I don't know at what prominence, a mark for the Humanitarian Law Fund. That's all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, do you still have a point to make or has it been covered? If it has, then we can hear from the general about his research overnight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to object to Mr. Nice's allegation that the book was written by OSCE. With all my experience and age, I still can't understand how OSCE can write a book. It's the same as saying that any document sent by whoever and published by the United Nations was written by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have some information about the book. It's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. General, you did some work overnight in relation to Mr. Ashdown's evidence, and would you like to tell us now what you found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, first of all, let me place this map that I received from Mr. Nice. It shows this same pointer stopped at Pecani village. Can I remove this now? Could I kindly ask you to let us see the video footage again today, and I'll explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If the control booth can identify the video, then it should be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if possible, could we freeze at two points. Could Mr. Nice possibly remember the day when this observation took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask if there is another case here this afternoon? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the second observation was on a day about, but I'll try and get the exact date, the 20th or a little later, in September. That's my recollection, and I'll just check if I've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one are we dealing with, Mr. Nice, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second one, I think, is the one the witness is concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on or after the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. I've got a copy of Lord Ashdown's published diaries, which refer to the 27th. So if that's material, I think it's probably the 27th, according to that book. At least for part of his observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the tape is -- the tape is ready now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the tape is being prepared -- "A. So I was positioned approximately here, near the village of Pecani. The -- as we calculated, the guns that were firing were up here, in the area of Blace. The villages we were looking at were the villages of Budakovo, which is here, through to Vranic, which is over here, Macitevo, which is here, and Kruscica, both Gornja Kruscica -- Gornja Kruscica is up here and Kruscica is down here."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, before the witness goes on reading through the diaries, it may actually not have been the Sunday but the Monday because the diaries begin with an explanation that he was going to find out what happened on the Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should need to go on viewing this film. Could we freeze it at the point when Lord Ashdown is watching through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right here. Right here, please. Mr. Nice, do you know what kind of binoculars Mr. Ashdown is using? What are its specifications? And could you please just pay attention to one thing: Above the arm of His Lordship, this area here, that's some sort of woods, you can see the road down there below, this is very important, Mr. Nice. It's very important for me to know the type of binoculars. Is it the military type of binoculars, and what kind of lens, what scale, and what is the magnifying power?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes as no surprise -- ah, there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. It's important for me to know the type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not matter of expertise for me. I know nothing of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that as far as you can take it, then, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on with the film, and then when it ends I will say. Can we see those houses in flame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I would like to know one thing: Was the TV crew positioned next to Lord Ashdown when they were filming this? This TV crew that filmed the lord, did they also film this house in the village, and which village was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are all questions that I'm afraid I'm not in a position to answer. I can -- it's a BBC film. It was a BBC film of the visit, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage can be relevant only if it was filmed from the point from which Lord Ashdown was observing. What am I trying to say? We can switch it off. We don't need it any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is a map that I made last night. It's a copy of a map that we have seen here, and as you can see the scale, topographic map 1:50000, Prizren-2, number 680-2. This is extremely important. Mr. Nice uses maps of unknown scale. Even the one we just saw a moment ago has an unidentified scale, and it's misleading me, the Trial Chamber, and everybody else. One of the principal characteristics of a map is the scale, because based on the scale you can deduce other things. The next thing Mr. Nice's map is lacking is the topographic feature. And when we are dealing with such sensitive issues, we should be using topographic maps of 1:50000 to 1:100000 scale. Last night I came to the conclusion that the maps used by Mr. Nice are approximately 1:250000 in scale, and they don't show relief. Mr. Ashdown pointed certain villages on the map. Since I didn't know where exactly he was standing, I assumed he was standing near the mosque in Pecani village, at an altitude of 480 metres. Let me just note that Mr. Ashdown was enjoying at the time the hospitality of our country whereas Pecani village was under terrorist control. So Mr. Ashdown mentioned the following villages: First, Macitevo village, which is about 13 kilometres away from the point where he was standing. The next one was Vranic village. It is at a distance of 10.5 kilometres. Next, Donja Kruscica, seven kilometres away from him. Next, Budakovo village, nine kilometres away. And he mentioned Gornja Kruscica at a distance of 10.5 kilometres from the place where Lord Ashdown was standing. So I tried then to depict this in a different way, assuming that he was in Pecani village. And by the way, I wanted to know the exact point where he was standing in order to make a topographic analysis of what was visible to him. But please, look: Pecani village, Vranic village. Vranic village was mentioned. I will show you how this looks in terms of altitude. Again we used this map and this scale. This is the mosque in Pecani village, altitude 480 metres, approximately. At a distance of 800 metres towards Vranic village, we have a feature. So at a distance of 800 metres from the mosque we have a feature, trig point 551. At a distance of seven kilometres, we have trig point 959. At a distance of 8.5 kilometres, we have a point at an altitude of 600 metres. And at nine kilometres we have a feature 751 metres high. So if you're standing here, in front of you is this hill. Then it's followed by valleys at Sentra [phoen], then Vranic 680 metres altitude. In front of Vranic is something that is 750 metres high. So from this point you cannot see Vranic village. I made the calculations. From this point Mr. Ashdown could see the industrial part of Suva Reka. He couldn't see Suva Reka, he could see the industrial area of Suva Reka. He could see these villages here going south towards Prizren. He could see a part of these villages to the south-east. And as for Macitevo, he could see only those things that are at an altitude over 1.100 metres. In Budakovo, which consists of five mahalas, he could see only two mahalas. The camera, if it was positioned here and if it was filming the first village here, Popovljanje and Dvorane with a mixed population Serb-Albanian, they are at a distance of 10.5 kilometres. That's why I would need to know which camera was used, because to film something that is 10.5 kilometres away and to see the windows on houses is simply impossible. Binoculars would have to have a range of 13 kilometres. All that seems impossible. I agree that up here on this territory there are points from which you can indeed see part of territories that are higher than what you can see from Pecani village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that in mind, it might help the witness that if this in fact the 27th of September, and the diary of course was not written for precision but if it was the 27th of -- for precision for Court purposes, it was precise for other reasons no doubt -- he describes heading south-west for Djakovica, rising up escarpment out of the town, stopping at a rubbish tip, and back up the hill in the sunlight, rounding a spur to see the whole of the Prizren valley. He could see -- the valley, he could see village after village burning. That's how he describes it in the book. I suspect, although I don't want to interrupt this long answer if it's helpful to the Court, but I suspect that if it's material, we have to get some more detail in one form or another from Lord Ashdown, and I'm sure he'll be prepared to provide it, 92 bis or in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that everything depends on exactly where he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think, incidentally, there's any suggestion that the -- that the burning window was necessarily part of the same sequence as the vision from a distance. It was simply part of the BBC's film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, we have taken some time with this now. Are you concluded? Because we are really beyond the time. I think we have the gist of the point that you wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was just one matter for clarification; whether we could be advised whether the burning window and building was inserted into the film at that point. That would be perhaps a useful matter of clarification that wasn't dealt with as part of Lord Ashdown's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, my conclusion is this: I completely challenge Mr. Ashdown's statement. What Mr. Nice just said, that he could see the Prizren valley, I completely agree with that. I say that he could see the entire Prizren valley as well from the area around the village of Pecani, but he could not see part of Suva Reka towards Budakovo, which is where the last stage of the anti-terrorist operation was under way. So my conclusion is that I cast absolute doubt on Mr. Ashdown's statement and testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that. I'd like to extend my apologies to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber. My colleagues will endure with me the raps on the knuckles which I undoubtedly will receive for this administrative breach. We are adjourned until Monday, Monday afternoon, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of July, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
